answers.brief_reasoning: Coulomb's law says the force is proportional to q1q2/r^2. The 1s electrons are closest to the nucleus, so r is smallest. Almost no other electrons shield them, so they feel nearly the full +13 nuclear charge. This gives them the strongest attraction, so they need the most energy to remove.
answers.final_answer: 1s electrons are closest to the nucleus and least shielded, so they have the greatest Coulombic attraction and the highest binding energy (151 MJ/mol).

answers.brief_reasoning: Si's valence electrons are also in n=3, so they are about the same distance from the nucleus and are shielded by the same core electrons (1s2 2s2 2p6). Si has 14 protons instead of 13, so its effective nuclear charge is greater. That means a stronger Coulombic attraction, which pulls the electrons closer and raises the binding energy. Taking the valence-electron peak to mean the outermost 3p peak, Si's is above 0.58 MJ/mol (its actual value is about 0.79 MJ/mol).
answers.final_answer: Higher: Si has one more proton but the same shell and core shielding, so its valence electrons feel a greater effective nuclear charge and are held more strongly.

answers.brief_reasoning: The Cl–F bonds are polar. In a T-shape the bond dipoles do not cancel, and the lone pairs make the molecule asymmetric, so there is a net dipole.
answers.final_answer: Polar

answers.brief_reasoning: Ethanol has an O–H bond, so its molecules can hydrogen bond with each other. Dimethyl ether has no H bonded to O, so it has only dipole–dipole and London forces. The London forces are similar because the molar masses and electron counts are the same. The stronger hydrogen bonds in ethanol need more energy to overcome, so ethanol boils at a higher temperature.
answers.final_answer: Ethanol's molecules hydrogen bond with each other (O–H), but dimethyl ether's cannot. Their London dispersion forces are similar, so ethanol's stronger IMFs give it the higher boiling point.
